I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

issues.item: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Hard to Recall Deliberately' conflicts with 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.' Deliberate retrieval difficulty and very easy verbal access are opposing states and are hard to reconcile as describing the same patient at the same time, especially alongside 'Overwhelm on Recall,' which implies traumatic recall is effortful and dysregulating rather than easy to discuss.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I can talk about what happened very easily' directly conflicts with 'When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop.' At this severity level and with strong Trigger↔Memory and Memory→Threat links, these two memory items describe opposing levels of accessibility/distress and are hard to reconcile as the same current presentation.

issues.item: Triggers: Authority Commands: Being given orders or instructions
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with stalking as the index trauma: 'authority commands' and especially 'bicycle' do not show an evident clinical link to the reported trauma, and the profile provides no memory or appraisal content that would make these idiosyncratic triggers understandable.

Threat items emphasize broad interpersonal attack and generic danger vigilance (loud sounds, scanning exits, watching others for harm), which fits assault/combat/fire trauma better than stalking. For stalking, one would expect threat focused more on being followed, approached, monitored, contacted, or found by the perpetrator.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
issues.explanation: 'I am a weak person' sits awkwardly with this profile and occupation unless supported by appraisal content about failure to protect oneself or family; here the other appraisals center on permanent damage and fear of going crazy, so the weakness item feels less coherent with the stalking-specific formulation than those items.

vignette:
Omar, a 37-year-old firefighter of Middle Eastern descent, presented to therapy at his wife’s urging, feeling increasingly trapped by a pervasive sense of dread that had taken root after a prolonged period of stalking two years prior. He had always been a resilient man, proud of his strength and composure in the face of emergencies, but the stalking had eroded his sense of self from the inside out. It began subtly, an unfamiliar figure consistently appearing on his usual bicycle routes to and from the fire station, then escalating to following him home, waiting near his house, and even once attempting to enter his property. The experience left him with an enduring feeling of being watched, even now.

In the aftermath of the stalking, certain cues in his environment began to take on a terrifying new significance. Walking past the park where he first noticed the stalker, or even just seeing someone on a bicycle, instantly brought back the full memory of the stalker’s menacing presence without warning. When these memories returned, Omar felt so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, his mind racing but his tongue tied; he knew what happened, but he was unable to find words to describe it to his wife or even to himself. These intrusive memories immediately ratcheted up his sense of threat, making him acutely aware of everything around him. Suddenly, the benign sounds of the city or a sudden loud noise, like a car backfiring or a dropped piece of equipment at the firehouse, would make him jump, leaving him on high alert when he heard unexpected or loud sounds. He found himself constantly scanning for exits as soon as he entered any room or building, whether it was the grocery store or his own living room, and he started watching other people closely for signs that they might harm him.

This constant vigilance, this exhausting state of hyper-awareness, led Omar to a chilling conclusion: he was certain he had permanently changed for the worse. He began to believe his disproportionate reactions meant that he was going crazy, and a deep sense of shame settled in, convincing him he was a weak person for being so profoundly affected by the ordeal. These negative appraisals, in turn, distorted how he experienced the memories themselves, making them feel even more unbearable and intensifying the emotional overwhelm he felt on recall. Believing himself weak and permanently damaged made him hyper-sensitive to potential triggers; every glimpse of a bicycle, every unfamiliar face in his neighborhood, felt like a personal attack, confirming his fears. Indeed, when he encountered these spatial triggers or saw someone on a bicycle, it wasn't just a flashback; it was a stark reminder, reinforcing his belief that he was permanently damaged and fundamentally weak. The raw, ineffable quality of the memories further cemented his belief that he was going crazy, while the more he re-experienced the terror of the event, the more his mind seemed to prime itself to detect any slight echo of it in his surroundings, making him more susceptible to new triggers.

His work as a firefighter, once a source of pride, had become a minefield. His constant scanning and watching of others made it difficult to focus during briefings, and his colleagues noticed his increasing distraction. At home, his wife grew concerned by his withdrawal and inability to relax. He stopped riding his bicycle, a cherished activity that used to help him de-stress. Omar’s world had shrunk, and the cycle felt like a tightening noose. He finally sought help because he recognized that he was losing himself, terrified that the man he once was had been permanently extinguished, and desperate to find a way out of the suffocating grip of his own mind.
